paragraphs: When Zhu Xu returned from Jiankang with the twenty-one-article draft, damp firewood was filling the Qin command tent with smoke. Fu Jian’s eyes were red from it, yet he examined every word whose ink showed a different hand. At the end stood the surnames of thirty-seven people who had taken part in the deliberations: nobles, ward heads, boatmen, the mother of a wounded soldier. Several had made only a mark, because they could not write.
Fu Rong tapped the final line of names. “Liu Yu has some nerve, sending these people to speak before the Heavenly King.”

“He is afraid you’ll hear no voice but his,” Zhu Xu said from a lower seat, his clothes not yet dry. “I ask Your Majesty first to suspend the building of additional siege engines, so the people inside know these words aren’t merely buying time for another assault.”

Some of the officers objected. Qin had barely secured its position south of the Yangtze; opening even one layer of the encirclement could admit reinforcements. Fu Jian agreed only to halt construction of new siege equipment. The existing camps would stay, weapons and armed vessels would still be barred, and merchant and medicine boats would be inspected and admitted under the established rules. Zhu Xu offered no words of gratitude. He wrote the decision in the record of exchanges. He told the officer at the camp gate that he had come to carry messages between two sides; if the Qin court required him to write “Zhu Xu, subject of Great Qin” on the documents, this journey would end. The officer issued him a Qin camp pass and continued to address him as “Master Zhu.”

The draft traveled back and forth between the banks for six days. The Secretariat at Chang’an, Xianyang Hall at Jiankang, the army’s granary office, and the household offices on either bank each sent proposed deletions and revisions. Some refused to put their names to the text. Others signed, then heard their estates might be audited and asked to withdraw their signatures.

Liu Yu put two incompatible county land registers into the same case and sent them across the river. The draft decree sent by Fu Hong from Chang’an carried, at its end, the grain office’s estimate of the costs of a three-year transition. A marginal note added: where the central treasury could not meet a need, Jiangnan should find its own resources, but no unapproved tax was to be levied privately. When Liu Yu read it, he circled “find its own resources” in thick black ink.

Not until the seventh day did they agree to hold the formal treaty conference and ceremony for the surrender of the seal at the Fei River. Fu Jian no longer wished to make the Jin court kneel outside Jiankang’s gates while Qin surrounded the city; the Jiangnan delegation likewise refused to remove its ancestral imperial seal atop a platform in the Qin camp. Jiankang lay several days' travel from the Fei. The two entourages set out north in sequence. Qin first removed several siege palisades outside the city and left the agreed number of soldiers to escort wounded men home. Liu Yu ordered Jingkou’s navy to guard the imperial delegation on its journey, forbidding its men to enter the Qin camp to drink and cause trouble.

In winter the Fei’s waters ran lower. The old gate of the northern camp had long vanished; the rotting stakes in the mud flats stood only a few inches high, and rusty nails still turned up from the earth. Following the old ritual for accepting surrender, the ceremonial officers built a platform three zhang tall on the shore and marked out positions for the imperial throne and for displaying prisoners. When Fu Jian arrived he saw craftsmen climbing a heavy wooden ladder, while a few hired river workers braced the posts below. He asked the officials whether the men with their feet in the mud would be able to see the words that were to be written upon the platform.
The ceremonial officers replied that receiving an imperial seal required a sovereign’s dignity. The people need only watch from afar.
Fu Jian pointed to the two highest levels they had just erected. “Take those down. Pay the craftsmen for both nights' work all the same.”

The remaining platform, three chi high, held a single long table. Qin banners to the north and Jin banners to the south still stood. Two tents beside the platform were reserved for the delegations to examine documents, and the credentials and numbers of guards had been checked against the earlier agreement. The two armies withdrew to their respective banks. Twelve guards from each side oversaw a central stretch of stony shore. Planks bridged a narrow channel; when the water rose, people had to stop and cross it step by step. Nobody could ride arrogantly up to the opposite party.

Fu Rong’s injured leg had not healed. Leaning on a staff, he mounted the low platform and saw an old ebony case at the corner of the table. He knew the crack in its lid. It held a handwritten letter left by Wang Meng during his final illness. The ink on the single sheet had faded almost to yellow: Do not attack Jin for ten years. Fu Rong replaced the paper and closed the lid.
“If Jinglüe could see us today, he might refuse to come.”
“I might not dare ask him to his face,” Fu Jian replied.

A horn sounded three times on the southern bank. Zhu Xu came first, accompanied by Liu Muzhi carrying the scrolls. Liu Yu followed from the ferry, his old armor dull with wear and no sword at his waist. He Wuji’s expression was grim among the ranks, while Meng Chang kept his gaze on the documents laid beside the table. Last came the Jin imperial kinsmen and ceremonial officers. Twelve men carried a black-lacquered chest holding the imperial seal, yellow silk bound at its corners. A young Keeper of Seals steadied the knots with both hands, his knuckles blue from the river wind.

A Qin ceremonial officer tried to begin with the rites of homage to the emperor. Sima Zun, the elderly head of the imperial clan, stood still and said the Jin emperor’s decree relinquishing his title had not yet been read aloud; he had come here as a Jin subject. Qin guards muttered in disapproval. Fu Jian allowed him to follow the old rites for envoys first, and the delegations exchanged deep bows. The difference between an old allegiance and a new one was a sheet of paper, yet nobody would hurry through those few moments.

Formal negotiations began before noon. Jiankang’s twenty-one articles had been reduced by Chang’an’s revisions to seventeen. Private notes, copies, and appended opinions had filled two large trunks over the past six days. Zhu Xu asked both delegations to argue from only one authorized copy, marked with signatures across its page joins. If wording changed there, clerks on both sides would copy the amendment at once and stamp it with temporary verification seals, lest another edict disappear without a trace.
Qin’s opening text read: From the day the imperial seal is presented, the former Jin prefectures and commanderies shall follow Qin’s calendar and be governed according to Qin law.

Liu Yu stopped his brush at the word “according.” Did that mean Guanzhong’s land measures would be brought to survey Wu Commandery’s flooded rice fields the very next morning? Would Jin’s old provisions for embankments, sluices, ancestral lands, marriage and inheritance all be abolished in a day? A Qin minister argued that there could not be two sets of law. Fu Rong feared most that delay would give local magnates time to conceal land and households.
“Laws can take time to settle,” Liu Yu said. “Killing people and taking their land cannot wait. Put down which laws will apply first.”

Fu Rong proposed immediate uniform rules for murder, theft, private armed forces, and grain robbery; commercial fraud and seizure of land by officials would be judged under shared criminal provisions. Liu Yu accepted, then added that existing local regulations for waterworks, lineage marriage and inheritance, and land taxation would remain provisionally in force for three years, subject to verification. At the end of that period the Jiangnan regional administration and Chang’an Secretariat would be required jointly to submit proposals for legal reform. When Zhu Xu heard “required to submit,” he told the clerk to write “required” with a firmer stroke. Fu Jian agreed.

The matter of the Jin imperial house was harder. Qin had drafted the words “Depose the Jin emperor and enfeoff him as Duke of Luling.” Sima Zun pointed to “depose.” The Jin ruler could relinquish the imperial title himself and ask that more fighting be spared, he said; but the Qin court could not erase his ancestors' memorial tablets from the paper along with his throne.
“The outcome is settled. What use is one word?” a Qin censor asked.

“None to the victor,” Sima Zun replied. “But I must take that word home. Only then will some of my kinsmen agree to open the ancestral temple themselves and announce the decree of relinquishment to the dead.”

Fu Jian changed “depose” to “relinquish of his own accord” and retained the title Duke of Luling already agreed between the two states. Qin’s ministers then insisted that the Sima princes could not privately recruit retainers or command provincial and commandery troops. The Jin envoys demanded that their families not be forcibly relocated, their tombs not disturbed, and their ancestral temples allowed to continue their rites. They signed each point in turn, without a single cry of celebration. Sima Zun kept his fingers on the paper until the last endorsement was sealed.

On landholding, Fu Rong offered two years without abrupt change; Liu Yu asked for five. They stared across the table while ink spread in a blot upon a clerk’s sleeve. Liu Yu admitted he lacked the force to guarantee every condition. Of his own accord, he dropped his demand that Jiangnan’s existing governors and magistrates remain in office for three years. Qin could review each official immediately, but replacement could not be used as a pretext for confiscating the land of ordinary subjects. In return Fu Rong agreed that for three years only disputed boundaries would be surveyed while existing cultivation continued; new transactions had to be entered in the registers of both administrations, so that no one could secretly give away or sell land during the audit.

An aristocratic aide standing behind Sima Zun was nearly beside himself with anger. His family had three estates stretching from East Mountain to Danyang, and he feared auditors would seize them under pretext of investigation. Liu Yu knew his concession would alienate many great clans that had supplied grain to defend the city. But if the old officials could never be replaced, all Chang’an would have won was a jade seal from a region still obeying its previous masters. In the end both sides recorded their opponents' names and objections at the end of the agreement, to be reviewed later.

The article on the Beifu Army could cause a mutiny if even half a sentence reached the barracks. Qin’s draft declared, “The Jin army shall surrender its arms and await disposition.” Liu Yu immediately pushed it back. Send those words to Jiankang, he said, and he could not persuade his former soldiers to leave their camps in peace.
“How, then, shall we draw up their rolls tomorrow?” Fu Rong asked.

Liu Yu laid out the three paths Liu Muzhi had prepared. Men who wished to return home would receive back pay before going back to their fields; those willing to farm garrison land would receive allotments verified by the regional administration; those who chose to join the new army would have their service and arrow wounds examined camp by camp, without being assigned lower status for having served in the southern army. Officers would be examined individually, and crimes dealt with according to law. A Qin general proposed abolishing the Beifu designation immediately. He Wuji suddenly set his teacup down hard.
“Xie Xuan’s banner flew over Jingkou for years. If you burn it today, in whose ancestral hall are the brothers to mourn their dead?”

Nobody spoke on the wooden platform. After a long silence He Wuji heard Liu Yu answer, “Seal away the old banner and preserve the army’s rolls of the dead. Let them put down their swords today. First pay the living households the grain and wages they’ve been owed for six years.”
“How much better is a banner in storage than a banner burned?”
“At least it still exists,” Liu Yu said.

He Wuji would have argued further. Then he saw the slight tremor in the hand with which Liu Yu held his brush. At last he left the table and walked back over the planks to the southern bank. Looking at that hand which had once wielded a sword beside his own, he swallowed the words at his lips. Liu Yu did not send anyone to stop him. He instructed the clerk to record Wuji’s refusal to sign.

After He Wuji had returned south, the article about sealing away the banner still lay on the table. Fu Rong asked an army clerk to fetch Jingkou’s old arrears ledger; its opening pages contained debts six years old. It took a long time for the delegations to agree: the camps would be reorganized and renamed over nine months; back pay would be issued and the dead accounted for before any men were sent home to farm. The old banner would be stored in Jingkou, not burned. Liu Yu also demanded the northern army’s lists of wounded and dead. Fu Rong tightened his lips, then told his attendants to bring the whole chest of northern military records onto the platform.

The dispute over household registration was equally stifling. Migrants who had come north had received government oxen and seed grain. If they now wished to return to their old homes, northern villagers resented seeing public property carried off with them. Yet how could families on the southern bank be kept apart across the river even after the war?

Zhu Xu took from his belt the old accounts of the relief boats and asked both sides to reckon the matter separately. People could take their own property. Oxen and seed grain received from the government could not be held as a pledge against their persons. Those who chose to return had to surrender their allotted wasteland; for public supplies not recovered, Jiangnan would compensate Qin in cloth, salt, or grain over five years. Old criminal cases would be checked against records on both banks, and no one could be detained as an alleged fugitive laborer without evidence. Sweat beaded on Liu Yu’s forehead, but he still signed the compensation clause.

By the time they argued over Liu Yu’s title, pain had brought sweat to Fu Rong’s temples. Qin’s draft called him “Great General Who Subdues the South.” Liu Yu circled the character for “subdues.” If he returned bearing that title, he said, Jingkou’s old soldiers would hardly see him as a man sent to settle the lives of the people. Fu Rong moved his staff an inch and told him to speak plainly.

“Let a provisional regional administration oversee the military and civil affairs of Jiangnan, with authority jointly confirmed by both sides,” Liu Yu said. “Three years. My troops cannot be mobilized on my order alone. I must be permitted to return one appointment from Chang’an for reconsideration; if the same appointment is made a second time, I shall comply. I shall not attend court regularly in Chang’an during the first year. From the second year I shall go once annually, publishing my itinerary beforehand.”

Qin’s ministers opposed any right of Jiangnan’s regional administration to return a court appointment. Liu Yu asked what he ought to do if a new official arrived and shut Jiangnan’s sluices, stopping boats from carrying grain: wait for Chang’an’s reply, or rescue the people below the embankment first? Fu Rong asked whether, in a military emergency, he could deliver a factual report within ten days. Liu Yu said he could. Fu Jian authorized a provisional Jiangnan administration for three years, allowed one request to reconsider an appointment, but required compliance if the appointment was repeated. Emergency deployments had to be reported, with supporting evidence, within ten days; violations on either side could be investigated. The words on the paper changed again and again. The clerks rubbed their stiff fingers and could barely keep hold of their brushes.
“And if you use these powers to rally your old army in revolt?” asked a military envoy sent by Fu Pi.
“The court has the right to investigate,” Liu Yu replied. “And if an inspector it sends abuses his authority against the people?”
“The Jiangnan administration may impeach him as well,” Fu Rong answered, instructing the clerk to write down both provisions.

No clause that day could claim an uncontested victory. At dusk the wind rose on both banks and fine sand gathered beside the inkstones. They settled on fourteen principal articles, with six separate implementation schedules covering military rolls, land, ferries, ancestral temples, compensation, and the provisional administration. Lest Qin and Jiangnan preserve different accounts of what they had agreed, the treaty was copied three times: one for Chang’an, one for Jiankang, and one for the witnessing officers at the river. Both sides signed and sealed the joins on every page. Zhu Xu read each clause aloud. Many still would not lift their heads.

It was near twilight when the Jin clan’s senior representative read the decree relinquishing the imperial title. In Jiankang, the Jin ruler had personally verified the text and sealed his decree at the ancestral temple. The copy on the platform bore the seal of state and the delegation’s certification; it was read publicly again today before both armies. As Sima Zun reached the passages relinquishing the imperial title and preserving the ancestral temples and tombs, his voice grew heavy. Former Jin subjects on the southern bank gradually knelt facing Jiankang. The young Keeper of Seals wiped his tears on his sleeve, afraid they would dampen the silk wrapping.

He lifted the lacquered chest. The planks shifted beneath him with a surge of water, and Liu Yu reached out to steady its base. “After this,” the boy whispered, “can we still call ourselves people of Jin?”
Liu Yu did not promise him a Jin palace rising anew. He said only, “No one can change where you were born, or what your parents were called.”
“And the name of the state?”
“After today, it will be gone.”

Slowly the boy set the chest upon the table. Sima Zun untied the vermilion cord and presented the jade seal. At last he performed the rites owed to the new dynasty before Fu Jian. When he straightened, his back remained perfectly upright. A Qin ceremonial officer raised the drumstick, but Fu Jian signaled him not to strike.

The jade had been polished smooth. It felt neither warm nor cold in his hand. For decades he had dreamed of gathering all under heaven beneath one seal. Now that he truly held it, he noticed a tiny chip on one corner, scarcely visible. Fu Jian did not lift it aloft for the crowd. He set it in the middle of the table, ordered the clerks of both sides to verify the old seal impression, and had the seal and decree placed together in a new case.

He opened the ebony case he had brought and set Wang Meng’s old promise not to attack Jin for ten years beside the jade. Fu Rong regarded the two objects without asking why the words of a dead man had been brought to accompany a kingdom’s farewell. When autumn winds in years past, and the spring winds of this year, crossed the river, soldiers had stood along its banks waiting for orders. The day they had not crossed the river had lengthened, year after year, into the road that led to this moment.

On the southern side, Jin’s banner was slowly lowered and folded by Sima Zun and the young Keeper of Seals. The old Beifu troops saluted with their weapons sheathed, then returned to their original camps; Qin troops were not permitted to enter and hurry them along. He Wuji did not return. As Liu Yu passed the ferry, Meng Chang offered no salute, saying only that he acknowledged defeat in war but still did not accept this unification.

“Keep that belief,” Liu Yu replied. He forbade his attendants to record Meng Chang’s breach of etiquette. If the treaty had promised that men would not be punished for service in the former army, and he began on the very first day to settle old scores, nobody would put down a sword tomorrow.

Night was coming, but the wooden platform still stood on the shingle. Fu Rong came beside Fu Jian, leaning on his staff. Across the river the camp lights shone on both banks. Guards were changing shifts; at the bridgehead, clerks continued checking the travel permits of people returning home.
“Imperial brother, have we won all under heaven?”
“We have received the seal.”
“You won’t even let a man rejoice for once.”

Fu Jian watched an old soldier on the opposite bank carry away a chest containing an old banner. After a long while he said, “If tomorrow a man takes this agreement to a county office to claim grain owed to him, and the magistrate recognizes it, then we shall have gained another inch.”

Fu Rong shook his head and smiled at his brother. As he turned, pain caught in his right leg, and he gripped the corner of the table. A gust lifted one corner of the treaty; beneath it stirred the sheet Wang Meng had left behind. Fu Jian laid his palm over it. When the wind died, he closed the case.
